back: The thermal decomposition of long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes (and sometimes hydrogen).
A high temperature (about 500 °C) and a catalyst such as aluminium oxide or silica.
Demand for petrol is greater than supply from distillation; alkenes are needed to make polymers and ethanol.
notes: Some cracking also gives hydrogen for making ammonia.
C and H must balance on both sides.

front: Why does cracking always give an alkene (or hydrogen)?
back: An alkane does not have enough hydrogen atoms for every product to be an alkane.

front: Test for the alkene made by cracking
back: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless.
Paraffin on ceramic wool, hot catalyst (broken porcelain or aluminium oxide) in the middle of the tube, gas collected over water.

front: Safety step at the end of the cracking experiment
back: Lift the delivery tube out of the water before you stop heating, to prevent suck-back.
Chemical: covalent bonds break and new substances (alkenes) form. Fractional distillation is physical.
